prompt: What type does subtracting one character literal from another, such as `'b' - 'a'`, have in Carbon, and why was it changed from what the character redesign first specified? Does the same now hold for subtracting two `char` values?
key: Written in proposals/p007314-charliteral-difference-should-be-an-intliteral.md (landed in #7314 on 2026-06-09). The char redesign (p006710) made `CharLiteral - CharLiteral` an `i32`, the smallest power-of-two type that holds any difference of values in [0, 0x10FFFF]. It is now `Core.IntLiteral`, evaluated at compile time. Two reasons. Consistency: operations on literals yield literal types, so the difference can be a template argument of type Core.IntLiteral and converts implicitly to any integer type that can hold its value (`var offset_u8: u8 = 'b' - 'a';` works, `'a' - 'b'` into a u8 is an error) instead of being locked to i32 and needing explicit, possibly lossy casts. Layering: `i32` is not primitive but an alias for `Core.Int(32)` defined in core/prelude/types/int.carbon, so defining CharLiteral arithmetic in core/prelude/operators/arithmetic.carbon would make it depend on a type not yet defined, a circular dependency that the orphan rule would force to be solved by reversing the edge and defining all Core.Int operations in arithmetic.carbon; IntLiteral keeps the integer types self-contained. `char - char` is unchanged and still produces `i32` (i9, i16 or i32 are left to a future proposal).

sources.quote: Change the result type `CharLiteral - CharLiteral` from `i32` to `Core.IntLiteral`.
In Carbon, operations on literals (like `IntLiteral - IntLiteral`) yield other literal types (such as `IntLiteral`).
should be implicitly convertible to any integer type (like `i64` or `u8`) depending on the value of the difference, rather than being locked to `i32`.
However, `i32` is not a primitive type; it is a type alias for `Core.Int(32)`, which is defined in `core/prelude/types/int.carbon`.
By producing `Core.IntLiteral`, we keep the integer types self-contained.
This proposal does not consider making any changes to the type of `char - char`, which will therefore continue to produce `i32`.

Gives the consistency reason: literal operations yield literal types, so the difference converts implicitly to any integer type that holds it (u8, i64) and can be a template argument, instead of being locked to i32

Gives the layering reason: i32 is Core.Int(32) from core/prelude/types/int.carbon, so CharLiteral arithmetic producing it would make the prelude's operators depend on a type defined later (a cycle the orphan rule makes awkward); IntLiteral keeps the integer types self-contained
